paragraphs: This paper asks whether accelerated optimization can carry over to curved spaces. In ordinary convex optimization, acceleration uses information from earlier gradient steps to improve progress. The corresponding question on a curved space concerns geodesically convex functions, whose convexity is defined along the space’s own shortest paths. The authors examine this question on the hyperbolic plane.

Their result establishes an obstruction: in the noisy setting studied, there is no counterpart of accelerated gradient descent for these functions on the hyperbolic plane. The conclusion applies even when the noise is exponentially small. Thus, the barrier does not require large errors that would obviously overwhelm an optimization procedure.

The proof intuition connects optimization to geometry. In negatively curved spaces, the volume inside a ball increases so rapidly that past gradients fail to provide useful information for future progress. This explains why importing acceleration from ordinary convex optimization faces a fundamental difficulty here. The theorem specifically concerns robust acceleration under noise in this geometry; its stated scope does not establish impossibility for every curved space or every noise-free formulation.
neurips-2021-a-no-go-theorem-for-robust-.tldr: The paper proves that even exponentially small noise can prevent an analogue of accelerated gradient descent on the hyperbolic plane.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn a population of reinforcement learning agents that behave differently while still earning high rewards. Its motivation is that diversity can support adaptation: when an environment changes, a population may already contain behavior suited to the new conditions. The learning objective therefore concerns a space of useful policies rather than a single policy.

The proposed method uses a generative model that maps a small latent representation into an agent policy. Different locations in this latent space correspond to different policies. This lets the system represent an entire population without maintaining separate policy parameters for each member, making the population’s diversity part of a shared generative representation.

Adaptation happens by selecting policies through their latent representations. The method can therefore respond to environmental changes solely through selection within the learned policy space. The authors test this capability in several environments, including an open-ended grid world and two-player soccer. The contribution is a way to combine policy diversity with a compact representation that supports adaptation through selection.
neurips-2021-adaptable-agent-populations.tldr: A generative policy model represents diverse agents in a compact latent space and adapts to environmental changes by selecting policies within it.

paragraphs: The paper addresses optimization problems whose objective is a sum of simpler submodular functions, each involving only a limited subset of the variables. It focuses on components determined by how many elements are selected, rather than their identities. This structure appears in applications including image segmentation and generalized cuts in hypergraphs.

The authors develop the first approximation algorithms for this particular problem. Their approach converts the objective into a sparse graph cut problem that can be computed quickly. The requested approximation factor controls the sparsity of the resulting graph, connecting the quality of the approximation to the size of the computational representation.

The central technical insight links sparse graph constructions with piecewise linear approximations of concave functions. This connection makes it possible to exploit the cardinality structure systematically. The resulting reductions improve theoretical running times and deliver substantial practical gains on image segmentation and hypergraph clustering tasks. The contribution is specifically an approximation approach for cardinality-based components, rather than a claim of faster exact minimization for every submodular objective.
neurips-2021-approximate-decomposable-su.tldr: The paper accelerates approximate minimization of cardinality-based submodular sums by reducing them to sparse graph cut problems.

paragraphs: Associative memory stores patterns and retrieves them when presented with an incomplete or corrupted cue. This paper proposes a neural implementation based on a hierarchical generative network that receives stimuli through sensory neurons. Its training uses predictive coding, an error-driven learning procedure inspired by cortical information processing.

The authors evaluate whether the network can recover stored patterns from damaged or partial inputs. Their comparisons include autoencoders trained through backpropagation and modern Hopfield networks. Across the reported retrieval experiments, the proposed model achieves better accuracy and robustness than these popular associative memory approaches.

One highlighted result concerns completing natural images, including images from ImageNet, when only a very small portion of the original pixels is available. The model retrieves these partial patterns with high accuracy in the reported experiments. Beyond retrieval performance, the authors present the architecture as a plausible framework for studying biological memory because its operation resembles the hippocampus acting as both an index and a generative model. This is a proposed explanatory framework for memory, rather than evidence that the model establishes how biological memory works.
neurips-2021-associative-memories-via-pr.tldr: A predictive-coding memory model improves retrieval from corrupted and incomplete inputs in comparisons with autoencoders and modern Hopfield networks.

paragraphs: CoAtNet addresses a trade-off between convolutional networks and Transformers for vision. The authors find that Transformers tend to offer greater model capacity, but their generalization can suffer without suitable built-in assumptions about images. The goal is to combine convolution’s useful inductive bias with attention’s capacity in a single family of models.

The design rests on two ideas. First, depthwise convolution and self-attention can be expressed within a shared relative-attention formulation. Second, arranging convolution layers and attention layers in a principled vertical stack improves generalization, capacity, and efficiency. This makes the organization of the hybrid architecture central to its reported benefits.

Experiments report strong results across datasets and resource constraints. CoAtNet reaches 86.0% ImageNet top-1 accuracy without extra data. With pretraining on 13 million ImageNet-21K images, it reaches 88.56%, matching the cited ViT-huge result using 23 times less pretraining data. Scaling with JFT-3B yields 90.88%. Together, these results support the authors’ claim that the hybrid design works effectively across substantially different data scales.
neurips-2021-coatnet-marrying-convolutio.tldr: CoAtNet combines convolution and attention to improve image recognition across different training-data and resource settings.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate the performance of a policy using previously collected contextual bandit data when each action contains several coordinated choices. Such actions are called slates and occur in recommendation systems and interface optimization. Evaluation becomes difficult because the number of possible combinations can grow extremely large.

An existing pseudoinverse estimator addresses this setting under an assumption that conditional average rewards are additive across actions. The authors use control variates to construct a broader family of unbiased estimators. This family contains the pseudoinverse estimator and, asymptotically, its self-normalized version, bringing these approaches into a common framework.

Optimizing within that family produces new estimators with guarantees of improved estimation risk over both existing versions. The point is to use the freedom within an unbiased estimator family to make evaluation more accurate, while retaining its statistical foundation. Experiments on synthetic data and real recommendation data support the improvements in practice. The additive-reward assumption is central context for the pseudoinverse approach on which this work builds.
neurips-2021-control-variates-for-slate-.tldr: Control variates yield slate-policy evaluators with guaranteed risk improvements over pseudoinverse estimators, supported by synthetic and recommendation-data experiments.

paragraphs: Anderson mixing had already been used heuristically to make reinforcement learning converge faster and use samples more efficiently. This paper develops a mathematical explanation for those benefits. It examines reinforcement learning through its fixed-point iterations: repeated updates that seek a solution unchanged by the update rule.

The analysis connects Anderson mixing to quasi-Newton optimization methods. It also proves that Anderson mixing enlarges the convergence radius of policy iteration schemes by an additional contraction factor. This concerns the region from which convergence can be obtained, giving a more precise account of the method’s benefits than empirical acceleration alone.

The authors also introduce a stabilization strategy combining a regularization term with a differentiable, non-expansive MellowMax operator. These modifications are intended to support both faster convergence and more stable behavior. Extensive experiments report improvements in convergence, stability, and reinforcement learning performance. The paper therefore contributes both an explanation of an existing acceleration idea and a modified method designed to make that idea more dependable in deep reinforcement learning.
neurips-2021-damped-anderson-mixing-for-.tldr: The paper explains Anderson mixing’s convergence benefits in reinforcement learning and introduces regularization and MellowMax to improve stability.

paragraphs: Visual question answering is intended to test reasoning about an image and a question together. However, a model may answer using recurring dataset associations, such as a frequent answer to a question, while overlooking the image. This paper addresses harmful biases in both language and vision, while recognizing that some learned regularities can help identify plausible answers.

The proposed D-VQA method works at the feature level and the training-sample level. It builds separate question-to-answer and vision-to-answer branches to capture biases associated with each input modality. Two unimodal detection modules then explicitly identify and remove negative biases, targeting the harmful associations rather than treating every regularity as undesirable.

At the sample level, D-VQA constructs two kinds of negative training examples without requiring extra annotations. These examples support the model’s training alongside the feature-based bias handling. Experiments on VQA-CP v2 and VQA v2 demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution is a combined treatment of language and visual shortcuts that also acknowledges the potential usefulness of legitimate patterns in the data.
neurips-2021-debiased-visual-question-an.tldr: D-VQA targets harmful language and visual biases using dedicated detection modules and negative training examples without additional annotations.

paragraphs: This paper examines an image property hidden in the features produced by deep classification networks. Small image patches are known to have similar statistical characteristics across scales. The authors find that distributions of deeper features instead change distinctively across scales, and they use these internal differences as an image fingerprint called deep self-dissimilarity.

The fingerprint supports image quality assessment in two settings: with a reference image and without one. Measures derived from deep self-dissimilarity correlate strongly with human preferences in the reported evaluation. This suggests that comparing how deep feature distributions vary across scales captures information relevant to perceived image quality.

The authors also use deep self-dissimilarity as a training loss for image restoration networks. The resulting restored images are reported to be at least as photorealistic as those produced by GAN-based methods, without requiring adversarial training. The same underlying property therefore serves both as an assessment tool and as a training signal. Its value lies in making internal differences across image scales useful for evaluating and improving visual results.
neurips-2021-deep-self-dissimilarities-a.tldr: Differences in deep image features across scales provide quality measures aligned with human preferences and a useful loss for photorealistic restoration.

paragraphs: Exploration is difficult when several reinforcement learning agents must coordinate their behavior. The paper proposes EMC, which combines curiosity-driven exploration with episodic memory. Its starting point is the individual utility functions used for local action selection in factorized multi-agent methods, commonly described as individual Q-values.

The authors argue that these Q-values represent local observation and action histories while also reflecting interactions between agents through centralized training. EMC uses errors in predicting individual Q-values as intrinsic rewards. Because changes in these values can reflect both unfamiliar states and other agents’ influence, the resulting curiosity signal can encourage coordinated exploration of new or promising situations.

Episodic memory complements exploration by reusing informative experiences that the agents have already encountered to strengthen policy training. The authors illustrate the approach with explanatory examples and evaluate it on difficult StarCraft II micromanagement tasks. They report significant improvements over state-of-the-art multi-agent baselines on those tasks. The contribution is a curiosity signal tied to learned multi-agent utilities, paired with memory that helps turn explored experience into improved behavior.
neurips-2021-episodic-multi-agent-reinfo.tldr: EMC combines prediction errors in individual agent utilities with episodic memory to improve coordinated exploration and performance on StarCraft II tasks.

paragraphs: Quasi-Newton methods can converge extremely quickly near a solution, but that advantage may emerge only late in training on a large dataset. This paper studies how to make use of that local speed throughout empirical risk minimization. Its strategy changes the size of the training problem as optimization proceeds.

The method first solves a problem defined by a smaller data subset, stopping at its statistical accuracy. It then increases the sample size geometrically and uses the previous solution to initialize the next problem. Each stage therefore starts from a solution to a closely related, smaller learning problem instead of beginning anew.

The theoretical guarantee is conditional on the initial sample size being sufficiently large. Under the stated setup, the iterates remain in neighborhoods where quasi-Newton methods converge superlinearly, and each subproblem reaches that fast convergence regime after at most three iterations. Experiments on several datasets support the analysis and show computational benefits. The result does not say every subproblem finishes in three iterations; it concerns how quickly the superlinear convergence behavior becomes available.
neurips-2021-exploiting-local-convergenc.tldr: Gradually enlarging the training sample lets quasi-Newton methods repeatedly exploit local superlinear convergence under the paper’s initial-sample condition.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning needs a reward signal that tells an agent which outcomes are desirable, but specifying that signal can be difficult. This paper studies a setting where information about rewards comes only from asking an expert. The expert might assess individual states or choose between two trajectories. Because this feedback is expensive, the goal is to learn a useful reward model with few queries.

The proposed method, Information Directed Reward Learning (IDRL), maintains a Bayesian reward model, representing uncertainty about the reward function. It selects questions to maximize information about differences in expected return between policies that could be optimal. This directs feedback toward uncertainty relevant to choosing how the agent should behave. A standard reinforcement learning algorithm can then use the learned reward model.

The approach matters because improving reward estimates and improving the resulting policy are different objectives. IDRL focuses on the latter and accommodates different kinds of expert questions. Across evaluations involving multiple environments and query types, the authors report similar or better performance with significantly fewer queries than prior active reward learning methods. These findings support selecting feedback for its usefulness in comparing promising policies.
neurips-2021-information-directed-reward.tldr: IDRL selects expert questions that clarify which promising policies have higher returns, achieving similar or better performance with significantly fewer queries in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Imitation learning can fail to transfer when observable features differ between training and deployment environments. A policy may copy correlations specific to the demonstrations rather than the structure driving expert decisions. This paper builds on the idea that an expert’s behavior often depends on a shared latent structure that remains stable across environments.

Invariant Causal Imitation Learning uses demonstrations from multiple environments to learn a common feature representation and an imitation policy based on it. To address differences in transition dynamics, it separates shared causal features from environment-specific noise representations. This separation aims to retain information useful across settings while distinguishing variation tied to particular training environments.

The method also models an energy associated with expert observations and regularizes the imitator to minimize the energy of its next state. This encourages the policy’s observations to match the expert’s observation distribution. Experiments in control and healthcare tasks show effective generalization to unseen environments. The reported contribution combines a stable causal representation with a constraint on the states the learned policy tends to reach.
neurips-2021-invariant-causal-imitation-.tldr: ICIL learns shared causal features from demonstrations across environments and uses expert-observation regularization to support transfer to unseen settings.

paragraphs: Text-based games require agents to understand and act through natural language while navigating worlds with many characters, places, and objects. Their quests can involve long sequences of dependent actions. This paper develops a world model that represents such environments as knowledge graphs, giving the model a structured description of the world it must track.

The model learns two tasks together: predicting how an action changes the graph and generating the natural-language actions relevant to the current context. The authors formulate both tasks as generating a set of sequences, using the structure already present in graph descriptions and action expressions. They introduce a multitask Transformer architecture and a corresponding training loss.

Evaluation includes a zero-shot ablation study in textual worlds not encountered previously. The proposed methodology significantly outperforms existing textual world-modeling techniques in that study, and the ablations support the importance of its individual contributions. The findings concern transferable world modeling: tracking consequences and producing relevant actions in unfamiliar worlds, which are key capabilities for an agent operating through text.
neurips-2021-learning-knowledge-graph-ba.tldr: A multitask Transformer learns graph changes and relevant text actions, improving world modeling in previously unseen text-based environments.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning can learn efficiently from limited real experience, but its performance depends on training choices that may need to change over time. This paper focuses on scheduling those choices, especially the proportion of real data used for policy optimization in Dyna-style methods. The question is how that proportion should evolve during training.

The authors first analyze the role of real data theoretically. Their analysis suggests that gradually increasing its share can improve performance. They then introduce AutoMBPO, a framework that automatically schedules this ratio and other training hyperparameters for model-based policy optimization, using MBPO as the representative algorithm.

On several continuous-control tasks, MBPO trained with AutoMBPO’s schedules significantly outperforms the original version. The learned real-data schedule also agrees with the direction suggested by the theoretical analysis. These results connect an explanation of why real data matters with an automated way to adjust its use. The findings support dynamic scheduling in the studied setting rather than establishing one universal schedule for every model-based reinforcement learning method.
neurips-2021-on-effective-scheduling-of-.tldr: AutoMBPO improves MBPO on continuous-control tasks by automatically scheduling training hyperparameters, including a real-data ratio consistent with theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection and lossless image compression can both use a probabilistic model trained on one dataset and evaluated on another. The model assigns likelihoods to new images, making its behavior under distribution changes relevant to both tasks. This paper defines generalization in terms of those likelihoods and investigates what drives it for image models.

The authors find that local image features dominate this form of out-of-distribution generalization. Motivated by that finding, they introduce a Local Autoregressive model that deliberately models only local features. The design follows directly from the analysis: it concentrates modeling on the information identified as most influential for likelihood generalization.

The model achieves reported state-of-the-art unsupervised out-of-distribution detection performance without adding extra data. The authors also use it to build NeLLoC, a lossless image compressor, and report state-of-the-art compression rates and model size. These results connect one modeling choice to two applications. The generalization claim is specifically framed through likelihood, which is the shared quantity linking detection and compression in this study.
neurips-2021-on-the-out-of-distribution-.tldr: A model focused exclusively on local image features achieves strong reported results in unsupervised distribution-shift detection and lossless compression.

paragraphs: Adding layers to a graph neural network does not necessarily improve its predictions. A common reason is over-smoothing, in which repeated processing makes node representations too similar. This paper proposes a family of graph network architectures designed to control that behavior, addressing a structural obstacle to effective deeper graph models.

The designs take inspiration from numerical methods for solving partial differential equations on manifolds. This connection supplies both an architectural foundation and a way to analyze how the networks behave. The aim is to make the evolution of graph representations understandable through related mathematical analysis while controlling smoothing through the network’s design.

An extensive experimental evaluation examines problems across different fields. The architectures match or improve on the reported state of the art for tasks usually handled by different specialized architectures. These findings support the usefulness of the proposed family across multiple kinds of graph problems. The contribution is therefore both a design approach to controlling over-smoothing and evidence that the resulting networks can work effectively beyond a single application.
neurips-2021-pde-gcn-novel-architectures.tldr: PDE-GCN uses numerical ideas from partial differential equations to control graph-network over-smoothing and achieve competitive results across multiple domains.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning mixtures of multivariate Gaussian distributions while satisfying approximate differential privacy. It focuses on axis-aligned Gaussian components and establishes the first private learning result for their unbounded mixtures, including the univariate case. The guarantee measures how closely the learned distribution approximates the target in total variation distance.

The authors provide sufficient sample bounds in terms of the number of mixture components, dimension, desired accuracy, and privacy parameters. They also obtain a stronger sufficient bound when every component has identity covariance. These are learning guarantees under specified distributional structure, with a separate improvement for the more restricted covariance setting.

The main technique is private list decoding. Given heavily corrupted samples from a distribution, a list-decoding algorithm outputs several candidates, with at least one approximating the target. The authors show that private list decodability of a distribution family is sufficient for privately learning its mixtures. They then establish this property for axis-aligned Gaussians. This turns a method for finding a useful candidate among several possibilities into a general route to private mixture learning.
neurips-2021-privately-learning-mixtures.tldr: Private list decoding provides a new route to learning unbounded mixtures of axis-aligned Gaussians with sufficient sample guarantees.

paragraphs: Combining neuroscience experiments can introduce systematic differences that obscure the biological signals researchers want to study. This paper develops a domain-adaptation framework for separating those sources of variation. Its implementation uses adversarial optimization to remove differences between experiments while preserving meaningful biological information.

The authors evaluate the method on two-photon recordings of retinal bipolar cells responding to visual stimuli. This dataset is useful because known cell-type signals coexist with substantial variation between experiments. In the supervised setting, the study examines whether cell-type classifiers generalize across experiments and checks their results against anatomical cell-type distributions obtained from electron microscopy.

The unsupervised setting instead produces adjusted data that can feed into arbitrary downstream analyses. Across both settings, the method achieves the best reported trade-off among the compared approaches between removing experimental variation and retaining biological signal. That balance is central: making experiments look alike is useful only if differences relevant to biology survive. The work offers a flexible way to integrate functional recordings while explicitly addressing this competing objective.
neurips-2021-removing-inter-experimental.tldr: An adversarial domain-adaptation method improves the trade-off between removing experimental variation and preserving biological signals in retinal recordings.

paragraphs: Learning from shared data raises two distinct concerns: protecting individual contributors’ information and resisting maliciously corrupted data. Addressing only one can leave the other unresolved. This paper studies both requirements together for the basic statistical task of estimating a mean from independently and identically distributed samples.

The authors introduce PRIME, which they describe as the first efficient algorithm to provide both privacy and robustness across a broad range of distributions. This establishes a computationally efficient route to joint protection, rather than requiring practitioners to choose between the two goals in the studied mean-estimation setting.

A second algorithm improves the sample requirement but takes exponential time. Its near-optimal statistical guarantee matches a known lower bound for private mean estimation without robustness. This shows that simultaneously obtaining privacy and robustness need not impose an extra statistical cost in the setting covered by the result. The distinction between the algorithms matters: the strongest sample guarantee belongs to the exponential-time method, while PRIME supplies the efficient approach. The paper separates what is statistically achievable from what its efficient algorithm achieves.
neurips-2021-robust-and-differentially-p.tldr: PRIME efficiently combines private and robust mean estimation, while an exponential-time method shows near-optimal sample guarantees without extra statistical cost for robustness.

paragraphs: Seasonal patterns in a data stream can change over time, making forecasting harder than simply learning one repeating cycle. This paper proposes Shifting Seasonal Matrix Factorization, or SSMF, to learn multiple seasonal patterns and switch between them as observations arrive. Forecasting taxi trips between departure and destination locations is one motivating example.

The method calls these different seasonal patterns regimes. It detects changes between regimes as the stream evolves and adapts its forecasts accordingly. A lossless data compression scheme supports the switching process without human intervention, making regime changes part of the automatic forecasting procedure rather than something an operator must specify.

SSMF operates online, with constant time and memory per observation as stated in the abstract. This makes its adaptation relevant to continuing streams rather than only fixed historical datasets. Experiments on three real-world streams show more accurate forecasts than the state-of-the-art baseline methods considered. The contribution combines multiple seasonal regimes, automatic switching, and bounded per-observation processing into one forecasting approach for evolving event data.
neurips-2021-ssmf-shifting-seasonal-matr.tldr: SSMF forecasts evolving data streams by automatically learning and switching seasonal regimes with constant per-observation time and memory.

paragraphs: Data augmentation can help reinforcement learning agents handle unfamiliar visual environments, but it can also make training less sample-efficient or cause it to diverge. This paper investigates that tension in common off-policy algorithms. The authors identify two instability problems that both originate in high-variance Q-targets, the targets used to train value estimates.

Based on this diagnosis, they propose a simple stabilization technique for learning under augmentation. They evaluate image-based reinforcement learning with convolutional networks and Vision Transformers on benchmarks based on the DeepMind Control Suite and on robotic manipulation tasks. This tests the approach across both visual architectures and task settings.

For convolutional networks, the method substantially improves stability and sample efficiency under augmentation. It also achieves generalization competitive with state-of-the-art image-based reinforcement learning methods in environments with unseen visuals. The authors show that the technique extends to Vision Transformer architectures and suggest that augmentation may be especially important there. The findings connect more stable value-learning targets with the ability to benefit from visually varied training inputs.
neurips-2021-stabilizing-deep-q-learning.tldr: Addressing high-variance Q-targets stabilizes augmented visual reinforcement learning and improves reported sample efficiency and generalization.

paragraphs: Feature-importance explanations often remove parts of an input and measure the resulting change in model confidence. This paper argues that the altered inputs can fall outside the model’s training distribution. Consequently, explanations and their scores can reflect model priors and random initialization in unintended ways, undermining the authors’ notion of social alignment.

The authors propose a simple training modification that produces more socially aligned explanations and evaluation measures. They also compare five ways to remove features, finding that some create more out-of-distribution inputs than others. This shows that the replacement procedure is part of the explanation problem, because it affects the inputs on which the model is being judged.

Finally, the paper introduces four search-based explanation methods and evaluates them on six text-classification datasets alongside strong baselines. Parallel Local Search is the only method that consistently beats random search in those experiments. Its gains over the second-best method reach 5.4 points for Sufficiency and 17 for Comprehensiveness. The results connect how explanations are searched for with whether their evaluation inputs are appropriate.
neurips-2021-the-out-of-distribution-pro.tldr: The paper addresses distribution shift caused by feature removal and introduces a search method that consistently outperforms random search in its text-classification experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies adversarial attacks and defenses through interactions among a neural network’s input variables. It examines interactions at multiple orders, distinguishing dependencies involving smaller groups of variables from those involving larger groups. The goal is to use this common language to explain both how perturbations mislead networks and where robustness comes from.

The authors find that attacks mainly alter high-order interactions to fool the network. They also find that robustness in adversarially trained networks comes from category-specific low-order interactions. These findings connect vulnerability and robustness to different parts of the same interaction-based description, rather than treating each attack or defense as an unrelated mechanism.

The proposed view offers a potential framework for explaining existing methods that improve robustness. The authors also report revising an earlier inaccurate interpretation of the shape bias of adversarially learned features. The contribution is primarily explanatory: it identifies interaction structure as a useful way to organize observations about attacks, adversarial training, and learned features. Its unifying role is presented as a potential approach, rather than a complete explanation of every adversarial phenomenon.
neurips-2021-towards-a-unified-game-theo.tldr: The paper links adversarial attacks mainly to high-order input interactions and adversarially trained robustness to category-specific low-order interactions.

paragraphs: Meta-learning evaluation can ask two different questions. In-distribution evaluation samples training and test tasks independently from the same task distribution. Out-of-distribution evaluation changes that relationship. This paper argues that distinguishing the two is essential because success under one evaluation setting need not imply success under the other.

The authors identify a mismatch between much meta-learning theory and common few-shot classification benchmarks. Theory often assumes the in-distribution setting, while benchmarks commonly generate training and test tasks from disjoint classes, making their evaluation out of distribution. Across numerous benchmarks, methods that perform better under the latter setting can perform significantly worse under the former.

The study also identifies difficulties within existing out-of-distribution evaluation: reliably selecting a model for a given method and consistently comparing different methods. It offers suggestions for constructing benchmarks that support in-distribution tests and more reliable out-of-distribution tests. The practical message is that benchmark construction determines which kind of generalization a result measures, and that rankings can change when the task-distribution relationship changes.
neurips-2021-two-sides-of-meta-learning-.tldr: Meta-learning method rankings can change between in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluation, motivating clearer and more reliable benchmark design.
